title: Caché - San Francisco
text: Design and development of French bistro in San Francisco.
label: Discover

details.box:
Overview

Timeline:

November 2024 - January 2025

Role:

Product Design (UX/UI) - Web Developer

Tools:

Figma, WordPress, HTML, CSS
details.txt:
Background & Challenge

Caché is a modern neighborhood bistro in San Francisco that blends a relaxed French bistro atmosphere with contemporary culinary experiences. The restaurant needed a digital presence that reflected its identity, provided essential information, and facilitated reservations while optimizing for both desktop and mobile users.

The challenge was to create a website that not only showcased the brand’s unique personality but also delivered a seamless user experience for customers seeking details about the menu, reservations, and events.

Understanding the Audience

Before opening Figma, I sat down with the owners to walk through a typical week at the restaurant: who books ahead, who walks in, who comes back. That conversation, combined with a look at comparable San Francisco bistro sites, shaped three audience groups I designed around:

  1. Local Residents & Tourists : Seeking an elevated but welcoming dining experience, usually deciding same-day or same-week.
  2. Food Enthusiasts & Millennials : Interested in modern gastronomy and natural wines, more likely to check the menu and Instagram before booking.
  3. Casual & Special Occasion Diners : Exploring options for brunch, happy hour, or dinner, often comparing a handful of restaurants before committing.

The common thread across all three was that people wanted to see the menu and make a reservation within a couple of taps, without digging through a cluttered homepage. That became the north star for the layout: menu and booking always one click away, never buried under marketing copy.

details.title: Design Approach & Strategy
lines: The design focused on elegance and warmth, capturing the bistro’s inviting yet sophisticated atmosphere. Key elements included:

1. Color Palette

    2. I selected a terra cotta shade (#B86C51) that evokes warmth and a natural feel, complemented by an off-white background (#FBEBD9) to create a clean and airy aesthetic.

1. Custom Logo Design

    2. Instead of using an existing font, I hand-wrote the restaurant’s name on paper, scanned it, and vectorized it to create a unique and personal brand identity. This gave the logo a handcrafted, distinctive feel.

details.txt:
1. Typography
    2. The main text fonts are Ruffina for its refined and expressive character, paired with Lato for a modern and highly readable contrast.
  2. Icons & Visual Accents
    3. I designed additional custom icons, including an Instagram logo, a fish, and a carrot, allowing flexibility for the client to add visual markers for social media, seafood, or vegetarian dishes.

Development & Implementation

Using WordPress as the CMS allowed for flexible content management while ensuring smooth performance. Custom HTML and CSS were incorporated to refine styling beyond standard templates, ensuring brand consistency. Specific optimizations included:
  • A fully responsive menu and booking system
  • Fast-loading pages with optimized media content
  • SEO best practices to enhance discoverability

away.title: Take-aways
away.text: The site launched with the menu and reservation flow front and center, which is exactly what the owners had asked for after seeing how many of their regulars were booking from their phones. Building the logo from a scanned, hand-written mark instead of a stock font turned out to be the detail people mentioned most, it gave the brand a handmade feel that matched the food. Working inside WordPress also meant the owners could update the menu themselves once I handed the site off, which mattered more to them long-term than any single design decision I made. If I revisited this project, I'd push for a short round of user testing with real diners before launch rather than relying on my own walkthroughs, since a couple of the reservation-flow tweaks I made post-launch would have surfaced earlier.

details.box:
Overview

Timeline:

July 2024 - August 2024

Role:

Co-Founder & CTO - Product Design, UX Research

Tools:

Figma, Flutter, Firebase
details.txt:
Context

TheCollectible is an entrepreneurial initiative I co-founded to create a user-friendly marketplace for art and collectibles. As CTO, I led the technical direction while actively contributing to UX research and design. This experience strengthened my ability to balance business strategy, user needs, and technical constraints.

Research identified key pain points: difficulty accessing art, evaluating collectibles, and navigating existing platforms. Users needed a trustworthy, intuitive marketplace with seamless transactions and curated content.

details.title: The Development
details.subtitle: The process followed a structured UX approach:
lines: • User Research & Strategy

I started with a round of interviews with people who collect art or one-off pieces, plus a short survey shared in a couple of collector communities. The recurring frustration was trust: people didn't know how to judge condition or authenticity from a listing, and they didn't know who to ask. That shaped two personas I designed around for the rest of the project: the 'Careful Collector', someone with disposable income who wants provenance and detail before they'll spend, and the 'Casual Browser', someone drawn in by a specific piece who needs the buying process explained in plain language. From there I mapped the user flow around a single goal: get a browser from a piece they like to a confident purchase without needing to message anyone first.
• Branding & Visual Identity

The brand needed to feel more like a gallery than a marketplace, so I leaned into a darker, editorial palette with a serif wordmark instead of the bright, high-contrast look most marketplace apps use. I built a small design system (type scale, spacing, component states) early on so the web and mobile builds wouldn't drift apart as the team grew.
• Wireframing & Prototyping

Low-fidelity wireframes came first, mostly to settle the listing page layout, since that's where the trust problem lived. The early version buried provenance and condition details below the fold; moving them up next to the price, before any high-fidelity work started, was the single biggest change to come out of this stage. I then built high-fidelity prototypes in Figma and walked a handful of collectors through them before any code was written.
• Technical Development

The platform was built in Flutter for a shared codebase across web and mobile, on top of a Firebase back end for auth, listings, and storage. As CTO I made the call to keep the stack small and boring on purpose, since we were a small team and I didn't want to be debugging infrastructure instead of shipping the listing flow.
• Testing & Refinement

The listing flow and search were the two areas that changed the most after early feedback. Search in particular needed filtering by medium and price range added earlier than planned, once it was clear people were arriving with a specific type of piece in mind rather than browsing everything.
• Deployment & Scaling

We launched with a small, invite-based seller pool so I could watch how real listings performed before opening things up. That let me catch a handful of edge cases in the listing form (multiple images, pricing in different currencies) before they became support tickets.

away.title: Takeaways
text: The biggest lesson from TheCollectible wasn't a design pattern, it was how much of the UX work turned out to be about trust rather than layout. Once I understood that collectors needed proof and context before they'd buy, most of the interface decisions followed naturally. Wearing both the CTO and design hats also taught me to pick fights carefully: I said no to a few feature ideas that would have looked good in a pitch deck but would have slowed down the one flow that actually mattered, getting from a listing to a confident purchase.

details.box:
Overview

Timeline:

January 2024 - August 2024

Role:

Web Developer

Tools:

PHP, Laravel, MySQL, Tailwind CSS, Alpine.js, SoundCloud API
details.txt:
Background & Challenge

The client wanted an online radio built around SoundCloud mixes, with a deliberately old-school, slightly chaotic feel: random backgrounds, a hue-shifting logo, playful button art. The visual direction and branding on this project came from my partner, my job was turning that into a real site the client could run day to day.

The brief also included self-management: the client wanted to add new mixes and swap background images without calling me every time. That made the real engineering problem the admin panel, not the player.

details.title: Two Versions, One Site
lines: The first version shipped in July 2024: a plain PHP and MySQL site running on Apache, built fast to get the client something real to test and use. Once it was clear the admin side needed to do more than a login form and a few uploads, I rebuilt the backend in Laravel over the following months, with Breeze handling authentication and a proper admin panel replacing the hand-rolled one.

details.title: What the Admin Panel Actually Does
details.subtitle: Once rebuilt in Laravel, the panel handled:
lines: • Track management
The admin pastes a raw SoundCloud link and the app parses the artist and title straight out of the URL, no manual data entry.
• Ad rotation
A separate pool of sponsor tracks plays between mixes, chosen by whichever has been played the least, so no single ad gets overplayed.
• Background management

The client uploads images directly, or drops a folder of files in and the app syncs them into the database. Every image gets resized and compressed automatically, including animated GIFs, since a couple of the backgrounds are old joke GIFs that needed to keep moving.
• Fallback handling
If the database connection drops, the site falls back to a maintenance page instead of crashing. A radio station going down felt worse than most sites going down.

details.txt:
The Player Itself

The public-facing side is plain JavaScript wrapped around the SoundCloud widget: play, pause, skip, and a volume control that occasionally lands on a joke value instead of a real percentage, since the client wanted the whole thing to feel a bit unserious. The logo and buttons get a random hue shift on load, and long track titles scroll like an old marquee instead of getting cut off. Ads are skipped on mobile on purpose, autoplaying a sponsor track over mobile data felt like the wrong default.

  1. Color Palette

    2. The palette stayed deliberately minimal, black and white with a single accent color, so the background images the client uploads through the admin panel stay the focal point instead of competing with the UI.

away.title: Takeaways
text: This project taught me when to rebuild instead of patch. The first PHP version got the client live fast, but once the admin requirements grew past a login form and a few uploads, hand-rolling that in plain PHP would have meant reinventing a framework badly. Moving to Laravel for the second version gave the client a panel that actually holds up: real authentication, validated uploads, and image processing that doesn't need me on call every time they want to add a background.
It's also the project where I got comfortable telling a client that a feature belongs behind a real framework instead of stacking more custom PHP on top of what was already there.
